turns.content: Two eclipsing binaries have sinusoidal, double-lined radial-velocity curves. System 1 has `P = 2 yr` and component semi-amplitudes `10` and `5 km/s`; system 2 has `P = 1 yr` and semi-amplitudes `15` and `10 km/s`. Treat both orbits as circular and nearly edge-on. Explain why both component amplitudes are needed to compare the total system masses.

Derive the circular double-lined-binary proportionality between total mass, orbital period, and the sum of the two radial-velocity semi-amplitudes. Which factors cancel when the two systems are compared under the shared inclination assumption?
Compute the summed radial-velocity semi-amplitude for each system and their dimensionless ratio, with system 1 in the numerator.
Use the period ratio and the cube of the summed-amplitude ratio to write an expression for `M_system1/M_system2` before evaluating it.
Evaluate that mass ratio to three significant figures and state which binary has the larger total mass.
Explain why the longer period of system 1 does not compensate for its smaller summed radial-velocity amplitude, referring to the different powers in the mass relation.
Check the numerical result by evaluating the period factor and the velocity-cube factor separately, then multiply them once more.
How should the result be qualified given that exact inclinations, eccentricities, and measurement uncertainties were not supplied?
Report `M_system1/M_system2` and interpret it in plain language as an assumption-dependent comparison of the two total masses.
